After investigating for about an hour, at around midnight, the officers saw a truck matching the description in the complaint in a residential driveway on the community territory. The truck was running with its lights on. The officers stepped onto the driveway to approach the truck and saw a man sleeping or passed out in the driver’s seat. The officers spent a few minutes knocking on the truck window, but the occupant, Mr. Singer, did not respond. When the officers opened the truck door to rouse Mr. Singer, they smelled a strong odour of alcohol coming from his breath. He seemed tired and had bloodshot eyes. At the officers’ request, Mr. Singer provided a roadside breath sample, which registered as a “fail”. He was then arrested and taken into custody, where he refused to provide a further breath sample.

facts.text: The officer observed a strong smell of alcohol from the individual.
facts.why_it_matters: A strong smell of alcohol is a relevant factor in establishing reasonable and probable grounds for suspecting alcohol consumption, which may support a breath test demand under s. 254(2) of the Criminal Code.
facts.if_changed: If the officer had not detected a smell of alcohol, this would weaken the basis for the breath test demand.

facts.text: The individual was in a parked, running vehicle.
facts.why_it_matters: The presence of the individual in a vehicle, even if parked, may be relevant to the officer's suspicion that the individual was operating or had control of the vehicle, which is a factor in the legal standard for a breath test demand.
facts.if_changed: If the individual was not in a vehicle, the legal basis for the breath test demand would be significantly weakened.

facts.text: The officer did not observe any other indicators of impairment.
facts.why_it_matters: The absence of other signs of impairment (e.g., erratic driving, slurred speech, bloodshot eyes) may affect the officer's ability to establish reasonable and probable grounds for the breath test demand.
facts.if_changed: If the officer had observed other indicators of impairment, this would strengthen the legal basis for the breath test demand.

facts.text: The officer did not take further investigative steps before demanding the breath test.
facts.why_it_matters: The lack of further investigation (e.g., checking for mouth alcohol, waiting for a period of time) may affect the validity of the breath test demand under the legal standard.
facts.if_changed: If the officer had taken further investigative steps, such as waiting 15 minutes to avoid mouth alcohol contamination, this could have strengthened the legal basis for the demand.

facts.text: The officer had no evidence of the individual consuming alcohol recently.
facts.why_it_matters: The absence of evidence that the individual had recently consumed alcohol may affect the officer's ability to establish reasonable and probable grounds for the breath test demand.
facts.if_changed: If the officer had evidence that the individual had recently consumed alcohol, this would strengthen the legal basis for the breath test demand.

facts.text: The officer did not wait 15 minutes before administering the breath test.
facts.why_it_matters: The absence of a 15-minute wait may raise concerns about the accuracy of the breath test, particularly if there is a risk of mouth alcohol contamination.
facts.if_changed: If the officer had waited 15 minutes, this could have improved the reliability of the breath test and strengthened the legal basis for the demand.

facts.if_changed: If the officer had observed the individual consuming alcohol or regurgitating, this would have raised concerns about the accuracy of the breath test and potentially affected the legal standard for the demand.

items.detail: The officer must observe signs of impairment, such as red and glassy eyes, slurred speech, or the smell of alcohol.

items.label: Is the breath test administered in accordance with procedural requirements?
items.detail: The officer must follow procedural requirements, such as using an approved screening device and ensuring the driver is not under the influence of mouth alcohol.

items.label: Is the breath test lawful?
items.detail: If the officer has reasonable suspicion, observes impairment, and follows procedural requirements, the breath test is lawful.

items.label: Is the breath test lawful?
items.detail: If the officer lacks reasonable suspicion or fails to follow procedural requirements, the breath test may be conditional or unlawful.

items.label: Are there no observations of impairment or alcohol consumption?

                  (2) Where a peace officer reasonably suspects that a person who is operating a motor vehicle or vessel or operating or assisting in the operation of an aircraft or of railway equipment or who has the care or control of a motor vehicle, vessel or aircraft or of railway equipment, whether it is in motion or not, has alcohol in the person's body, the peace officer may, by demand made to that person, require the person to provide forthwith such a sample of breath as in the opinion of the peace officer is necessary to enable a proper analysis of the breath to be made by means of an approved screening device and, where necessary, to accompany the peace officer for the purpose of enabling such a sample of breath to be taken.

respondent was observed driving his motor vehicle in an
erratic manner in the centre of the street by a policeman
on bicycle patrol.  The vehicle was swerving from side to
side and the policeman gave chase on his bicycle.  The
respondent slowed down but failed to stop for an
uncontrolled intersection.  The officer caught up with the
vehicle, rapped on the window and signalled the driver to
stop.  When the respondent opened the window, the police
officer noted the respondent smelled of alcohol, his eyes
were bloodshot and his speech was slurred.  The police
officer immediately made a demand for a breath sample for
the purpose of analysis, which the respondent refused.  He
was subsequently charged and convicted of refusing to
provide a sample of breath for the purpose of analysis,
contrary to s. 254(5) of the Code and operating a motor
vehicle while disqualified from doing so, contrary to s.
259(4) of the Code.  It is the sentence for these two
offences the Crown seeks leave to appeal.
